title: CI/CD and GitHub Actions Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment, pipeline stages and triggers, artifacts and caching, and how a GitHub Actions workflow is built. Ends with the common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: CI vs Delivery vs Deployment
points: Continuous integration: merge small changes to the main branch often, and every push automatically builds and runs tests
Continuous delivery: every passing build is releasable, and a human approves the production release
Continuous deployment: every passing build goes to production automatically, with no manual gate
Comparison row: the three differ only in the last step (CI stops at tested, delivery waits for approval, deployment auto-releases)
The pipeline is fail-fast: a red stage stops everything after it, and a broken main branch is fixed before new work

chapters.title: Pipeline Stages and Triggers
points: Typical stage order: checkout → install → lint → test → build → package → deploy staging → deploy production
Cheap, fast checks (lint, unit tests) run first so failures surface early
Trigger on: push, pull_request, schedule (cron), workflow_dispatch (manual) and release
Filter triggers with branches, tags and paths so docs-only changes do not run the full pipeline
Gate production with an environment that requires approval, and use needs: to order jobs

chapters.title: GitHub Actions Workflow Anatomy
points: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/; it contains jobs, and each job contains steps
Jobs run in parallel on separate runners (runs-on: ubuntu-latest) unless chained with needs:
A step is either uses: (a reusable action, pinned like actions/checkout@v4) or run: (a shell command)
Minimal example: on: [push] → jobs: test: → steps: checkout, setup-node, run: npm ci, run: npm test
Pass config with env:, secrets.NAME and the matrix: strategy for running across versions or operating systems

chapters.title: Artifacts and Caching
points: Artifacts are build outputs (a binary, a test report) saved with actions/upload-artifact and fetched in a later job with download-artifact
Jobs run on fresh runners and share no files, so passing a build between jobs requires an artifact
A cache stores dependencies to speed up runs: actions/cache with a path: and a key:
Build the cache key from the lockfile hash, such as hashFiles('**/package-lock.json'), plus restore-keys: as a fallback
Comparison row: artifacts are the output of a run and are kept for download, while caches are inputs reused to save time and can be evicted

chapters.title: Common CI/CD Mistakes
points: Cache key without a lockfile hash: stale dependencies are restored, or the cache never updates
Hardcoded secrets in YAML or logs: use the secrets store, and forked PRs do not receive secrets
Unpinned actions (@main) or a floating latest runner: builds break unexpectedly, so pin versions or a SHA
Missing needs: lets deploy start before tests pass, and a missing permissions: block gives the token more access than the job needs
Slow, flaky pipelines get ignored: parallelise jobs, cache dependencies and fix or quarantine flaky tests

chapters.title: CI/CD Cheat Sheet
points: CI = build and test on every push; Delivery = releasable plus manual approval; Deployment = auto-release
Workflow file: .github/workflows/*.yml → on → jobs → runs-on → steps (uses / run)
Triggers: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch; filter by branches, tags and paths
Sharing: needs: orders jobs, artifacts pass files between jobs, actions/cache with a lockfile-hash key speeds up installs
Safety: secrets store, pinned action versions, least-privilege permissions, an approval environment for production
